node.label: Donald Creighton
node.date_label: The Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence 1937 · Dominion of the North 1944 · John A. Macdonald 1952, 1955 · CHA presidential address 1957 · “The Decline and Fall of the Empire of the St. Lawrence” 1969 · Canada’s First Century 1970
node.description: A Toronto historian whose The Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence (1937) built Canadian history around the one river system 'that leads from the Atlantic Seaboard to the heart of the continent', which inspired Canadians 'to build a great territorial empire, both commercial and political, in the western interior' (his own restatement of 1969); Dominion of the North (1944) calls the river 'the natural basis of a great commercial empire' and beaver fur 'the first staple of the St. Lawrence commercial system'. His two-volume John A. Macdonald (1952, 1955) completed what he called 'a trilogy on one theme'; in 1969 he accepted 'the parentage of an idea' others called 'the Laurentian interpretation of Canadian history', but rejected the story that his first book was 'the fruit of my friendship with Harold Innis'. As president of the Canadian Historical Association (1957) he attacked the Liberal 'Authorized Version' of Canadian history and the imported 'Marxian doctrine of the class struggle' and 'Frontier thesis', and in 1969 he traced the 'decline and fall' of the Empire of the St. Lawrence and of the Canada built on it, calling official bilingualism and a special position for Quebec 'a repudiation of the intentions of the Fathers of Confederation'. Contested in period: Michel Brunet (1953) found the Macdonald biography full of 'nombreux préjugés', Guy Frégault (1955) asked 'où sont les Canadiens français dans tout cela ?', and W. L. Morton, as Davis (1985) reports him, held that the metropolitan view he associated with Creighton seemed 'necessarily to minimize the importance of the hinterland'. From the late 1960s the national frame the Laurentian narrative supported gave way to regional history and 'limited identities' (Buckner, 2000).

node.scope_note: This entry presents the Laurentian narrative and Creighton's later nationalism. Read on 2026-10-14: his 1957 presidential address (pp. 1–12) and his 1969 lecture 'The Decline and Fall of the Empire of the St. Lawrence' (pp. 14–25), both in full from page images; Dominion of the North (1944) at its contents and selected pages (pp. 21, 24–25, 166, 270, 272, 298, 419, 505–507) in an open Internet Archive copy. The Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence (1937) itself is unread: the Internet Archive copies are borrow-only, and its argument is checked through the 1944 book, his own 1969 retrospect (labelled as such) and the first page of Herbert Heaton's 1938 review. He is not presented as the founder of a school: in 1969 he reported that others regarded the 1937 phrase as 'the inspiration, at least in part, of a new school' and the 'genesis' of 'the Laurentian interpretation', and said only that he had 'no wish to disavow the parentage of an idea'. The Innis lineage is recorded as contested: readers from Woodcock (1979) and Ouellet (1984) to Salmon (1997) tie the book to Innis's staple studies, while Creighton said the subject was suggested by W. P. M. Kennedy, 'not by Harold Innis, whom I barely knew at the time'. The 1957 and 1969 texts are polemics; their judgements of Mackenzie King, Quebec and bilingualism are recorded as his claims, not adopted. Morton's 'Clio in Canada' (1946) and his later hinterland critique are known here only through Davis (1985); Careless's 'Frontierism, Metropolitanism' (1954), Berger's chapter on Creighton (1976), Canada's First Century (1970) and the Innis biography (1957) are unread (catalogue or review level only). Canonical-work review (2026-10-24): added titles and dates are selected bibliography, not a complete career or a new reading of the books. Original works, translations, edited collections and posthumous editions are distinguished; earlier argument and source-reading qualifications remain.

incident_edges.relationship: The Laurentian narrative: the St. Lawrence commercial system as the basis of a transcontinental Canada (1937), carried through Dominion of the North (1944) and the Macdonald biography (1952–55)
incident_edges.evidence_note: In-period, his own text. Dominion of the North (1944; pages read in an open copy): the post at Quebec gave the French 'the one great river system which led to the Atlantic seaboard from the heart of the continent'; 'Inevitably the river came to seem the natural basis of a great commercial empire stretching far into the distant west; and the achievement of this empire became the common objective of successive generations of Canadians, though their methods altered and the staple products of their trade were sometimes changed. The first staple of the St. Lawrence commercial system was beaver fur' (p. 21); the rivalry of 'the northern and southern routes, between Montreal and New York, for the control of the Great Lakes system and the command of the western trade', a conflict that 'was to remain essentially the same' (pp. 24–25); 'Quebec had been the origin of the empire of the St. Lawrence; it was to be the genesis of the Dominion of Canada' (p. 298). In-period reception. Herbert Heaton's review (CJEPS, 1938; first page, p. 565, read) quotes the book as 'an attempt to trace the relations between the commercial system of the St. Lawrence and the political development of Canada' (the book's words as Heaton quotes them; the 1937 book is unread) and reads it as a test of the economic interpretation of history that 'has pleased neither the Marxians nor their enemies'. Michel Brunet (RHAF, 1953, p. 579) calls him 'l'un des maîtres contemporains de l'historiographie anglo-canadienne'; Guy Frégault (RHAF, 1955, p. 446) sums up the Macdonald biography as 'Nationalisme antiaméricain, impérialisme et centralisation : synthèse canadienne, — je veux dire anglo-canadienne'. His own retrospect, 1969 (read in full; a later statement by the author, not evidence of what the 1937 book says): 'This Laurentian theme has its basis in the fact that the St. Lawrence is the one great river system that leads from the Atlantic Seaboard to the heart of the continent of North America'; the river 'has inspired generations of Canadians to build a great territorial empire, both commercial and political, in the western interior of the continent' (p. 16); 'The west, it was believed, would make Canada a nation, and the east-west axis would be its backbone' (p. 17); in choosing Macdonald he had 'stumbled upon the only satisfactory method of writing the second phase', so that he had written 'a trilogy on one theme' (p. 16). The phrase, he says, came to be regarded 'as the inspiration, at least in part, of a new school of Canadian historians and as the genesis of a new historical doctrine, the Laurentian interpretation of Canadian history'; he had 'no wish to disavow the parentage of an idea' (p. 14). Later readings: Ouellet (1984, pp. 226–227) calls him 'le chef de l'Ecole laurentienne'; Salmon (1997) says he 'simplified and expanded Innis' thesis'. Contested in period: Brunet found French-Canadian newspapers unread ('Il n'a pas jugé nécessaire de dépouiller un seul journal canadien-français', p. 580) and 'nombreux préjugés' (p. 581); Frégault asked 'où sont les Canadiens français dans tout cela ? Tout simplement, ils n'y sont pas' (p. 447), while praising the work as 'fondé sur une compréhension exacte de l'histoire du Canada' (p. 444); W. L. Morton, as quoted by Davis (1985), saw in Creighton 'the preponderant role commercial monopoly and centralized business have played' (Davis, p. 97) and held that the metropolitan thesis, which he associated with Creighton and Careless, 'seems necessarily to minimize the importance of the hinterland' (Davis, p. 98); the critic George Woodcock (1979, p. 140) called his treatment of Confederation as centralist 'a major distortion'. A contribution, not a founding.

incident_edges.relationship: Innis's staple studies as a resource for Creighton's Laurentian narrative, as Creighton's own staple vocabulary and later readers show; Creighton rejected the story that the 1937 book grew from their friendship
incident_edges.evidence_note: His own texts. Dominion of the North (1944) frames the St. Lawrence system by its staples ('The first staple of the St. Lawrence commercial system was beaver fur', p. 21), and its reading list (pp. 505–507) names Innis's The Fur Trade in Canada (1930) and The Cod Fisheries (1940). The 1957 presidential address recalls 'the 1930's, when the influence of Harold Innis was at its height and everybody was writing and talking about staple production' (p. 3), and exempts Innis from the Marxian fashion: 'most of the professional economists — and especially Innis — refused to accept the simplified Marxian version of historical determinism' (p. 6). In 1957 he also published Harold Adams Innis: Portrait of a Scholar (unread); Benoît Brouillette's review (1957, p. 529, read) reports Creighton's account of Innis's Canada as an east–west system 'marqué par le Saint-Laurent et les Grands-Lacs', at once 'transocéanique et transcontinental'. The qualification, his own (1969, pp. 14–15): 'The Empire of the St. Lawrence, it is sometimes confidently asserted, was the fruit of my friendship with Harold Innis ... These explanations, like most simple generalizations, happen to be wrong'; the subject was suggested 'not by Harold Innis, whom I barely knew at the time, but by W. P. M. Kennedy', and he was 'reluctantly convinced by the weight of his own evidence' about the Montreal merchants (p. 16). Readers: George Woodcock (1979, p. 134): 'Creighton's master was H. A. Innis, especially the Innis of The Fur Trade in Canada, which contained the essential germ out of which — with Innis's encouragement — Creighton built the scenario of his first book'; Fernand Ouellet (1984, p. 226): Creighton started 'partant de la théorie des staples'; Deborah Harrison (1981), as quoted by Davis (1985, p. 97): 'probably the first to advance a metropolitanist interpretation, although the closely related "staples" thesis had been put forward by Innis much earlier'; Salmon (1997): he 'simplified and expanded Innis' thesis'. The edge records Innis's work as a resource the Laurentian narrative used, not a teacher–pupil derivation; Creighton's denial concerns the origin of the subject, not the use of the staple framework.

incident_edges.relationship: Turner's frontier thesis, as taken up by Canadian historians in the 1930s and 1940s, rejected as an imported 'continental revelation' that Canadian history would not fit (1957)
incident_edges.evidence_note: His own text, the 1957 CHA presidential address (read in full). Canadian historians had 'accepted, for historical purposes, the two highly fashionable political theories which dominated the thought of the inter-war and war years': 'the Marxian doctrine of the class struggle' and 'the Frontier Theory' (p. 6). Of the second: 'Turner ... fixed upon the movement of settlement across the continent as the most important fact in its history'; 'the source of creative inspiration and action was found not at the centre, but at the periphery, of western culture' (p. 8). Applied to Canada, 'painful difficulties were immediately encountered': the frontier's progress 'had been evidently modified by all sorts of extraneous and unnatural things such as railways, efficient police, governmental supervision'; in 1837 'the rebels had come, not from the frontier, but from the older settled parts of the province'; yet its believers 'kept insisting that Canadian democracy was "forest-born"' (p. 9). He ends: historians bought 'a couple of suits of imported intellectual reach-me-downs' and a new generation would show 'less deference for imported theories of historical change and more respect for the manifold facts of Canadian experience' (p. 12). The critique inverts his own Laurentian premise, that change radiates from the centre. Limits: the address is a polemic and names no Canadian frontierist; Turner is not quoted beyond the phrases Creighton cites, and the atlas's own reading of Turner (progressive/multiple_hypotheses) shows him advocating multiple hypotheses rather than a single doctrine. Context: Careless's 1954 CHR article, unread here, was 'conceived in part as an obituary for the frontier thesis of Frederick Jackson Turner' (Davis 1985, p. 95). No in-period reply to the address was looked for.

incident_edges.relationship: Creighton's characterisation of post-Conquest French Canada as a decadent feudal society, cited approvingly by Ouellet and Hamelin in the 1962 crisis article
incident_edges.evidence_note: Ouellet and Hamelin (1962, p. 32, read): the crisis reveals two cultural entities of unequal evolution, 'C'est pourquoi le professeur Creighton a pu parler, en se référant à la société canadienne-française, de société féodale décadente.' Ouellet's own 1984 survey (recorded by the 1.136 Creighton packet, pp. 226–227; not re-read here) summarises Creighton's post-Conquest French Canada as 'une société semi-féodale décadente devenue hostile aux impératifs économiques'. In-period critics pair them: Paquet and Wallot (1972, p. 186 n. 5) cite 'D. G. Creighton, The Empire of the St. Lawrence (2e éd., Toronto, 1956) et F. Ouellet, Histoire économique et sociale du Québec' as the 'historiographie traditionnelle' that saw restructurings but not modernisation; Tousignant (1980, p. 416) says the 1966 book 'faisait écho aux vieux préjugés de l'historiographie canadienne-anglaise' (no historian named). The influence rests on the 1962 citation alone; the critics' pairing and Ouellet's 1984 comparison are context and do not independently establish transmission. The edge records a borrowed characterisation, not a teacher–pupil lineage; Ouellet's Labroussian method has other sources (edge_874; edge 6).

named_group_routes.relationship: Antimodernism and the invented folk in twentieth-century Nova Scotia (1992, 1994)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period evidence (1992, 1994). In 'Tartanism Triumphant' (Acadiensis, 1992; pp. 5–9 read) McKay asks how Nova Scotia 'became Scottish' in the second quarter of the twentieth century, when 'a collection of hazy generalizations and ethnic stereotypes' became 'a natural and obvious "commonsense"'. His broad answer: 'it was part of an international anti-modernist wave, a local version of a general middle-class search for something outside and better than the crisis-ridden modern world it inhabited' (pp. 8–9); the narrow answer is the state's cultural power under Angus L. Macdonald. Note 12 takes Lears's definition of American antimodernism and adds the 'simple life' and 'nature'. The Quest of the Folk (1994) is checked at summary and contents level: chapters on 'The Idea of the Folk', Helen Creighton and folklore, Mary Black and handicrafts, the simple life, and the folk 'under conditions of postmodernity'. Muise's review essay (Acadiensis, 1998; pp. 128–32 read) describes the three case studies and quotes the book's conclusion that 'the concept of the Folk was and remains a powerful obstacle to the formation of a counter-hegemonic cultural politics' (p. 306). Wright's 1995 Acadiensis review essay on English-Canadian intellectual history cites the book for 'a very skilled handling of Antonio Gramsci's theory of cultural hegemony by an historian' (p. 132 n. 29). A contribution to the field's cultural strand, not its origin: Berger, McKillop and Owram precede it. In the sampled corpus, 56 of 1,303 strict History doctoral dissertations dated 2009–2026 cite the book. Bibliographies record consultation, not influence. In the Province of History (2010, with Bates) is a later reading.

named_group_routes.relationship: Staples history as a disputed Canadian antecedent of environmental history: Cook's continuity claim (1990) and Forkey's rejection (1998)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period texts first; they disagree. (1) Continuity: Ramsay Cook's W. L. Morton Lecture (1990; JCS 25:4, 1990–91) claims a long Canadian concern with environment: 'In a broad sense the writing of Canadian history has always been concerned with the environment' (p. 6). Against reading the older historians as nationalists only, he writes that nationalism 'was not a full-time interest for any of them. Certainly not Harold Innis for whom the fur trade, the cod fisheries and other staple products were the real stuff of history' (p. 6). He also marks a break: 'Innis, Lower and Creighton also struggled with the question of the impact of the North American environment on European women and men', but 'for this earlier generation of historians the exploitation of the environment was accepted as natural and necessary, even though excesses might be deplored' (pp. 6–7), and 'More recent environmental historians have a different focus' (p. 7). (2) Rejection: Neil Forkey (CHR 79:1, 1998) rejects the line: 'Although the environment was an ingredient in the work of Harold A. Innis, Donald Creighton, and Arthur R.M. Lower, their studies do not serve as prototypes for Canadian environmental history'; 'In their approach, the environment exists only as a scaffolding on which human history unfolds, and not as an actor in the process' (p. 70). 'The staples model masks the essential role of social relationships and the dynamic between humans and nature', and 'More appropriate antecedents' are found in the historical geographer Andrew H. Clark (p. 71; n. 6 cites The Fur Trade in Canada and The Cod Fisheries). Classification: 'influence' here records a proposed antecedent that Canadian environmental historians disputed, not an established transmission of method; no in-period text read shows environmental historians taking up staples method, and neither position is presented as the Canadian field's. Later readings (2003–2024), labelled as such and not the evidence this edge rests on: Graeme Wynn (2003 review, p. 96) agrees that Forkey is right 'to puncture' claims 'that the staples approach represents an indigenous form of proto-environmental history'; Wynn (2004, p. 33) writes that the staples works 'focused on human uses of the environment', with 'little concern in this work for the reciprocity and mutuality of relations between people and nature'. Tina Loo (2014, p. 622) reclaims the work: 'it could be argued that some of the most influential work on the country's past was a kind of global environmental history, even if its practitioners did not call it that', naming Innis and Lower. Daniel Macfarlane's entry in NiCHE's 'Crash Course in Canadian Environmental History' (2024) holds that Innis's legacy 'still shapes many key debates and approaches in contemporary Canadian environmental history' and that, through works such as Cronon's Nature's Metropolis, the staples and metropolitan-hinterland theses 'are perhaps Canada's biggest contribution to international environmental history'. The edge records a proposed antecedent the field disagreed over; it does not say that Innis wrote environmental history or founded the field. Innis's books are unread here.

named_group_routes.relationship: The English-Canadian national tradition analysed as historiography: its major figures, their nationalism and its limits (1976; 2nd ed. 1986)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own statement (1976 preface, reprinted 1986; Google Books snippet view of the 1986 second edition (volume jRN6AAAAMAAJ, University of Michigan copy; preface page not reported by Google), with the 1976 edition (bix6AAAAMAAJ) checked for the preface opening and contents. Snippets are short fragments; the continuous text was not read): 'This study is an examination of aspects of English-Canadian historical thought and literature since the turn of the century. It deals with the central teachings of the major figures - George Wrong, Adam Shortt, Chester Martin, Harold Innis, Arthur Lower, Frank Underhill, Donald Creighton and William Morton - and also, in a less detailed fashion, with a more numerous group of other professional scholars who shaped the way Canadians understood their past'; 'The main emphasis is on the creative edge of historical writing and on those authors who broke the traditional patterns of interpretation'; 'Written history represents a self-conscious effort to establish the meaning of experience for the present'. The 1976 conclusion, as Allen Mills quotes it (CJPST 1977, pp. 134–137, read in full): 'Canada's historians have all been nationalists of various hues, and sometimes their judgments about what was central to the past and what was peripheral arose as much from divergent conceptions of nationality as from disagreements about interpretations of the same evidence' (p. 259; Mills p. 136). The 1986 edition replaces that conclusion with a chapter on 'the vast exfoliation of historical literature over the last twenty years' (preface to the second edition). There 'A few historians in the sixties, moreover, subjected the tradition in which they had grown up to searching criticism. J.M.S. Careless joined Ramsay Cook in condemning the undue emphasis on national history and unity' (p. 261), and he quotes Careless (1969) that the 'nation-building approach' 'neglects and obscures even while it explains and illuminates' (p. 262); social history's 'initial impact was to magnify the diversity of Canadian history' (p. 298). In-period reception. Mills: the book 'makes a substantial contribution to the intellectual history of English Canada' and 'is really about' its eight 'superluminaries' (p. 135); 'his description of all Canadian historians as nationalists places much too much weight on that over-used term', since they 'have very different conceptions of the nation that is to survive' (p. 136); but 'Berger's claim that Canadian historians have been generally unconcerned to explore the group loyalties of class, region, culture and family is unimpeachable' (pp. 136–137). Terry Cook (Archivaria 5, 1977–78, pp. 198–203, read in full) calls it 'a remarkably subtle analysis of major trends in Canadian historiography' that 'transcends historiography to become an intellectual history of English Canada in the twentieth century' (p. 202). (Cook gives the 'nation-building' passage at p. 263 of the 1976 edition without naming Careless; the 1986 text attributes it to Careless.) Karr (1989, p. 161): 'As a sequel he analysed the national conceptual frameworks in which professional historians functioned and wrote.' The French-Canadian limit is his own choice, explained in the preface: 'two language traditions have, in historical thought as well as in other non-political spheres, occasionally touched and intersected, but in general they have been preoccupied with the backgrounds of two rather different “nations”', and a comparison 'must rest on preliminary appraisals of the individual traditions'; 'the two traditions of historical writing flowed in separate channels' (p. 181). Ronald Rudin (1997; snippet view) shares 'Berger's belief that historical writing can “reveal a good deal about the intellectual climate in which it was composed”' but does 'not accept his assumption, implicit in Writing of Canadian History, that historians across the twentieth century have been united by their search for the truth' (p. 4), and finds that 'Berger failed, however, to consider the way in which Groulx had, by the 1930s, altered his view of the Dollard affair' (p. 58). Gregory Kealey (1982, reprinted 1995; snippet view) notes that the Marxist Stanley Ryerson 'was not considered for systematic evaluation in The Writing of Canadian History' (1995, p. 84), while finding 'little to argue with' in Berger's 1986 summary of the labour-history debate (1995, p. 18).

named_group_routes.relationship: The Laurentian view criticised as regional rather than national, and the national school read as superseded (1977–83)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Cook's own words, read in full. 'The Burden of Regionalism' (Acadiensis 7:1, 1977, p. 110): 'The so-called national schools have, in reality, had a rather obviously regional focus. Those who live in the Valley of the Fraser, the Red or the Restigouche can hardly accept the Laurentian view of Canadian history as “national”, unless, of course, they are content to be considered as “colonials” — a point made long ago by W. L. Morton. And the other nationalist themes fare little better.' 'Regionalism Unmasked' (Acadiensis 13:1, 1983, p. 137): 'the so-called “national” approach to the interpretation of the Canadian past has come under a destructive barrage of criticism' (the decade before it is garbled in the text layer); Berger's The Writing of Canadian History (1976) 'might be viewed as a lengthy epitaph on the headstone of the national school's grave'; Morton's 'Clio in Canada' (1946) 'made explicit what had long been implicit in the Innis-Creighton laurentian thesis: the metropolitan-hinterland relationship was not one of equality'. In-period context: Buckner (2000, pp. 4–5) sets limited identities (edge 1) against a post-war consensus of 'liberal nationalists such as A.R.M. Lower and Frank Underhill' and 'conservative nationalists such as Donald Creighton and C.P. Stacey' for whom the nation-state was the frame of reference. Limits: Cook credits the point to Morton; he co-wrote a Centenary Series volume (1974); and by Buckner's account (p. 8) he 'warned regional historians of the danger of ignoring the “national experience”' in 1977 ('The Golden Age of Canadian Historical Writing', Historical Reflections; unread here). The critique is of the Laurentian claim to speak for the nation, not of the staple studies' economics. edge_805 (cdn_regional → cdn_national_tradition, critique) carries the regional historians' version of the argument.

named_group_routes.relationship: Metropolitanism: Canadian history read through metropolitan centres that organize frontiers and hinterlands, proposed as a wider framework than the frontier-environmentalist reading (1954)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own in-period statement. 'Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History', Canadian Historical Review 35:1 (1954), pp. 1–21, read in full in an Internet Archive scan of the issue. He sorts English-Canadian historiography into 'schools', 'merely for convenience' (p. 2): a Britannic school, a School of Political Nationhood, and 'the Environmentalist School, or North Americans All', which 'built particularly on the concept of the frontier in North American history derived from Turner' (p. 5); he names Munro, Underhill, Sage, Lower, Landon, A. S. Morton and A. L. Burt, adding that 'no tight determinism is intended in thus naming these authors, nor, on the whole, did they display any' (p. 6, n. 6). He finds in them 'a certain tendency to fix values', so that western farmers were 'Good' and eastern business men 'Evil' (p. 12), and 'a tendency to overvalue the influence of native North American forces and the material environment, and a tendency to undervalue forces transferred from Europe and the non-material environment' (pp. 13–14); 'while in no way underrating the very great contributions which frontierism and environmentalism have made', it 'does seem necessary to look for a wider framework' (p. 14). The Laurentian school of Innis and Creighton offered 'a metropolitan rather than a frontier viewpoint', and 'The result was virtually to establish “metropolitanism” in Canadian historiography' (p. 16). The metropolis is 'a city of outstanding size' dominating 'other cities and their countrysides, the whole area being organized by the metropolis, through control of communications, trade, and finance, into one economic and social unit' (p. 17), in 'almost a feudal chain of vassalage' (p. 17); 'the rise of metropolitanism is the other side of the coin to frontier expansion' (p. 18). His examples include the Clear Grits organized around Toronto, the Globe and George Brown (p. 19). He limits the claim: 'if we reject a frontier determinism we should hardly replace it with a metropolitan determinism' (p. 19), and concedes that a metropolitan interpretation may 'only restate old problems in somewhat different terms. It may be so: but what is particularly needed is a restatement' (p. 21). A contribution, not a founding: he credits Lower's Colony to Nation and essays, Masters's The Rise of Toronto (1947) and its source in Gras (p. 17, nn. 30–31), and the Laurentian school (p. 16). In-period reception and criticism, from Donald F. Davis, Urban History Review 14:2 (1985), pp. 95–113, read in full: the article 'heralded the arrival of “metropolitanism” as a “vitalizing approach”'; 'few other journal articles have been more widely cited or more frequently quoted' (p. 95); for most historians it became, in Carl Berger's words as Davis quotes them, 'the programmatic statement of the metropolitan approach' (pp. 95–96). Davis quotes W. L. Morton's objection that the metropolitan thesis, 'which he associated with both Creighton and Careless', 'seems necessarily to minimize the importance of the hinterland' (p. 98), and S. D. His own texts. 1962 (with Hamelin, read): French-Canadian historiography reflects 'les réactions émotives des classes dirigeantes canadiennes-françaises', and its simplifications result 'à la fois du mépris de l'économique et de l'idéalisation du fait politique' (p. 32; no historian is named). 1976 (read): 'Si notre « habitant » a subi un traumatisme, ce n'est pas au moment de la conquête mais au moment où le système agricole traditionnel ne peut plus fonctionner comme autrefois' (p. 116). 1985 (read): 'pour Maurice Séguin, théoricien de l'École néo-nationaliste', the leadership of New France belonged to the bourgeoisie, 'de sorte que la décapitation s'était exercée sur l'élite nationale elle-même' (p. 18); 'Cette thèse avait été épousée par Michel Brunet dès les années 1950'; in the 1970s 'la thèse de la dégradation de la bourgeoisie avait besoin d'être dédramatisée', and 'Ces retouches au modèle de Maurice Séguin furent faites par Gilles Paquet et Jean-Pierre Wallot, en particulier' (p. 19); at the core of the crisis controversy stood 'la thèse néo-nationaliste enrichie de l'idée de modernité' (p. 25). Séguin has no entry, so the edge targets the montreal_school strand. The modernists. His own text, 1985 (read for pp. 11–29 and the pages named): the dominant preoccupation of most of those who built the new economic history 'était par trop centrée sur la situation précaire des Canadiens français en Amérique du Nord', a feeling 'pas étranger à la montée du mouvement indépendantiste québécois'; the themes of dependence, of Quebec's lag behind Ontario and of francophone inferiority 'imprègnent d'une façon ou d'une autre une grande partie de cette historiographie', and 'ces préoccupations ont entraîné les historiens à négliger des secteurs entiers de l'histoire économique et, par conséquent, à se fermer nombre de voies d'accès à une explication du social' (p. 18); after Paquet and Wallot's 'retouches au modèle de Maurice Séguin' (p. 19), 'On peut en dire presque autant des études de Jean-Claude Robert, de Paul-André Linteau et même de Normand Séguin sur le caractère dynamique de la bourgeoisie foncière rurale et urbaine' (pp. 19–20). named_group_routes.relationship: In a critique of Pentland's Labour and Capital in Canada, the staples tradition's trade-centred economy faulted for confining attention to relations of exchange and passing over the household subsistence production that, he argued, made up most of early Canada's economy (1985)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own words (Labour/Le Travail 15, 1985, read in full), in a critique of H. C. Pentland's Labour and Capital in Canada, 1650–1860 (written 1960, published 1981), which is not an atlas entry: Pentland 'follows the lead of his Toronto mentors in conflating the Canadian economy and its overseas trade'; 'While Innis, Creighton, and their contemporary disciples confine their attention to relations of exchange, however, Pentland at least focuses on the ‘social relations of production’', so 'it seems fair to regard him as the labour historian of the staples school' (p. 9).
